title: Making plans together
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: THE noi ENDING IS ALSO THE SUGGESTION. Andiamo! is both "we go" and "let's go"; Facciamo alle sette is "let's make it seven". Italian needs no extra word where English needs "let's" and Spanish reaches for vamos a — the -iamo ending does the whole job, and it is the same ending on every verb: andiamo, facciamo, prendiamo, mangiamo, vediamo.

Ti va di…? is the everyday invitation, and its shape is one the learner already owns: literally "does it suit you to…", built exactly like L1-M1's mi piace. The thing offered is the subject and the person is named by the little word in front — so ti va di prendere un caffè, and nothing about it is new except the words.

THE ARTICLE ON A DAY MEANS "EVERY". il lunedì is Mondays in general; lunedì on its own is this coming Monday. English marks that difference with a plural — "on Mondays" against "on Monday" — and Italian marks it with an article, which is why L1-M4's il lunedì and this module's bare lunedì are two different things.

The clock adds e mezza, e un quarto and in punto to L1-M4's alle sette. The quarter-to form uses meno, and this course does not show it here: meno is M9's key and its first note has to be the comparative one. When M9 opens it, the clock use comes with it.

Plans are made among friends, so this module runs on tu and noi and the polite third person is deliberately absent. An invitation in the Lei forms is not wrong — it is a business appointment, which is M7's scene rather than this one.

sentences.cue: Shall we go to the cinema tonight?

words.note: One form, two jobs. As a question it invites; as a shout it means "come on". Nothing distinguishes them but the tone.

words.cue: we do · we make · let's make it
words.note: The noi cell of L1-M6's fare. Facciamo alle sette is how a time gets settled, and it is the same "let's" reading.

sentences.trap: There is no word for "let's" and none is missing. The ending carries the suggestion, which makes this one of the few places Italian is shorter than English.
sentences.sound: an-DYA-mo. Four vowels, three syllables — the ia is one glide.

variations.cue: Shall we go to the bar tonight?
Shall we go to Rome tomorrow?
variations.changed: a city, which takes a with no article

variations.cue: Shall we go to the cinema tomorrow?

mistake.why: a and il fuse: Andiamo al cinema stasera?

sentences.usage: Suggesting something to a friend. Among strangers this would be forward rather than rude.

sentences.display: Ti va di prendere un caffè?
sentences.literal: To-you it-goes of to-take a coffee?

words.cue: do you fancy · does that suit you
words.note: One thing, built like mi piace: what is offered is the subject and ti names who it is offered to. An infinitive follows, joined by di.

sentences.trap: The di is compulsory before the verb and disappears before a noun: Ti va di prendere un caffè? but Ti va un caffè? Both are ordinary, and only the thing that follows decides.
sentences.sound: tee VA dee PREN-de-re. The whole opener runs as one word before the verb.

variations.display: Ti va di mangiare una pizza?
Ti va di andare al cinema?
variations.cue: Do you fancy going to the cinema?

mistake.why: A verb needs di: Ti va di prendere un caffè?

sentences.usage: The lightest invitation there is — easy to accept and easy to turn down.
sentences.mnemonic: di before a verb, nothing before a noun.

words.cue: see you · we'll see each other
words.note: The closing every plan ends on. Literally "we see each other", and it is said as one thing — Ci vediamo! on its own is a goodbye.
The same particle family as M4's si, and it does several jobs. L1-M7's c'è and ci sono contain it and are their own whole surfaces, answering for nothing outside themselves.
The noi cell of L1-M6's vedere. On its own Vediamo means "we'll see", which is what an Italian says instead of committing.

sentences.trap: ci goes in front of the verb, exactly as M5's clitics do. It is the same placement rule, on a word that does a different job.
sentences.sound: chee ve-DYA-mo. The ci is a soft ch, and the whole phrase runs together.

variations.changed: a day instead of an hour

variations.display: Ci vediamo alle sette in punto

mistake.why: The particle goes in front: Ci vediamo alle sette.

sentences.usage: Ending a conversation once a plan is made — and it is a goodbye on its own.

words.note: Stressed on the last syllable, and every day from Monday to Friday ends that way — the -dì is "day". Days are not capitalised in Italian.
The same -dì ending. The stress on the end is what an English speaker gets wrong, saying mer-CO-le-di instead of mer-co-le-DI.

sentences.trap: There is no preposition in front of the day. English needs "on Tuesday" and Italian puts the bare word in — adding in or a is the error.
sentences.sound: mar-te-DEE. The accent on the ì is not decoration: it says the stress is on that vowel.

mistake.why: A day takes no preposition: Sei libero martedì?

sentences.usage: The question that opens every plan.
sentences.mnemonic: No preposition in front of a day.

sentences.cue: Let's make it half past seven

words.note: Feminine because it agrees with the hour, which is feminine — le sette. The zz is a long ts.
Masculine, so un quarto rather than una. The quarter-TO form uses meno, which M9 opens.
In punto means exactly on the hour. It is the noun for a full stop and for a point in a game, all from the same idea.
The gio is a soft j, and the stress is on the last syllable like every other weekday name.

sentences.trap: Facciamo here is not "we make" but "let's make it" — settling a time. It is the noi ending doing the suggestion job again, on a verb English would not use at all.
sentences.sound: fat-CHA-mo AL-le SET-te e MED-dza. Three double consonants in one line, all held.

variations.display: Facciamo alle sette e un quarto
variations.cue: Let's make it a quarter past seven

variations.changed: a day and an hour together

mistake.why: It agrees with the hour: alle sette e mezza.

sentences.usage: Settling the time, which in Italy happens after the day and not before it.

words.note: The last of the -dì days. Its name is Venus's day, as the French vendredi is.
The only day that is FEMININE and the only one not ending in -dì — so la domenica, not il. Saturday, sabato, is masculine like the rest.

sentences.trap: domenica breaks two patterns at once: it is feminine and it has no -dì. Both matter, because the article that means "every" has to agree — la domenica, il venerdì.
sentences.sound: do-ME-ni-ca. The stress is on the second syllable, unlike every weekday name around it.

variations.cue: On Sunday we're going to the cinema
variations.changed: a plan rather than an availability

mistake.why: domenica is feminine: la domenica — and here no article at all.

sentences.usage: Answering about a day, or offering one.
sentences.mnemonic: Six days in -dì, and Sunday is the exception.

words.note: An elision, so ONE index key — di plus accordo, welded. It is what you say when a plan is settled, and Va bene does the same job more casually.

sentences.trap: The apostrophe fuses the two words into one, exactly as in M5's dell'acqua and M4's l'angolo. There is no separate accordo to reach for here.
sentences.sound: dak-KOR-do. The double k is held, and the whole thing is three syllables.

variations.cue: All right, see you on Friday

mistake.why: The elision is compulsory: D'accordo, ci vediamo domani.

sentences.usage: Closing the deal, once the day and the hour are fixed.
sentences.mnemonic: One word, one apostrophe, plan settled.

words.note: The noi cell of L1-M3's mangiare, and the gi stays soft: man-JA-mo. Like andiamo, it can be a statement or a suggestion.

sentences.trap: This is a present tense doing the work of English's future, exactly as M5's Prendo did. Anything arranged goes in the present, and the time word carries the future all by itself.
sentences.sound: man-JA-mo. Three syllables, the gi soft, and the stress in the middle.

variations.cue: Shall we eat at home tomorrow?
variations.changed: the suggestion reading, as a question

variations.cue: On Sunday we're eating at home

mistake.why: a casa takes no article: Stasera mangiamo a casa.

sentences.usage: Settling what happens tonight — and the same words could be a suggestion.

sentences.display: Il lunedì lavoro, ma lunedì sono libero
sentences.cue: I work on Mondays, but I'm free this Monday
sentences.literal: The Monday I-work, but Monday I-am free

words.note: Bare, it means the next one. L1-M4's il lunedì, with the article, means Mondays in general — two different things sharing one word.

sentences.trap: The whole difference is one article, and English marks it with a plural instead. il lunedì is every Monday; lunedì is the one coming up, and no other word in the sentence changes.
sentences.sound: loo-ne-DEE. Stress on the last syllable, as the accent says.

variations.display: Il sabato lavoro, ma sabato sono libero
variations.cue: I work on Saturdays, but I'm free this Saturday
variations.changed: a different day, the same contrast

mistake.display: Lunedì lavoro, ma il lunedì sono libero
mistake.why: The article marks the habit: Il lunedì lavoro, ma lunedì sono libero.

sentences.usage: Sorting out which Monday is meant — which is exactly where this trips people.
sentences.mnemonic: Article means every. Bare means next.

sentences.cue: Let's take the bus at seven

words.note: The noi cell of L1-M6's prendere. The whole -iamo family is regular, which is why this module can add five of them at once.

sentences.trap: Every verb in this module ends -iamo and none of them is irregular there. The noi cell is the one place Italian's conjugations agree with each other.
sentences.sound: pren-DYA-mo. The ia is one glide, and the stress lands on it.

variations.cue: Let's take the train at seven
variations.changed: a different vehicle, with no elision

mistake.why: A vowel takes the elided article: Prendiamo l'autobus alle sette.

sentences.usage: Deciding how to get there, once the time is fixed.
